---
title: "Example: isochrones by mode"
description: >
  Areas reached from one point in Porto Alegre within 10, 20 and 30 minutes,
  walking, cycling, driving and by public transport.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 8.4, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
```

An isochrone is the area within a given travel time of a point. This example
draws them for the four ways of travelling peabiru routes, from one park in
Porto Alegre, and shows how far each mode gets in 10, 20 and 30 minutes.
Everything below is one script; the output shown is the output it prints.

## The data

The example uses the Porto Alegre sample of r5r 2.5.0: an OpenStreetMap
extract of the city, the GTFS feeds of its buses (EPTC) and of its
metropolitan train (Trensurb), a hexagonal grid with population, jobs and
schools, and a few points of interest. The files are downloaded once, into a
temporary directory (about 2 MB).

```{r download, message = FALSE}
library(peabiru)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

poa <- file.path(tempdir(), "poa")
dir.create(poa, showWarnings = FALSE)
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for (f in c("poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip",
            "poa_hexgrid.csv", "poa_points_of_interest.csv")) {
  if (!file.exists(file.path(poa, f))) {
    download.file(paste0(url, f), file.path(poa, f), mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
}

network <- build_network(poa)
network
```

The bus feed of the sample only has trips between late morning and early
evening on weekdays, so public transport is routed at 14:00 on a Monday.

```{r origin}
poi <- read.csv(file.path(poa, "poa_points_of_interest.csv"))
park <- poi[poi$id == "farroupilha_park", ]
park
departure <- as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")
```

## Isochrones, mode by mode

`isochrone()` returns an `sf` data frame with one polygon per origin and
cutoff. The polygons are made from a grid of travel times; `zoom` sets how
fine that grid is (from 9 to 12; at 11 a cell is about 65 m wide here). With
public transport, the travel time of each cell is the median over the
departures of `time_window`, here the 30 minutes from 14:00.

```{r isochrones}
modes <- list(
  "Walking" = "WALK",
  "Cycling" = "BICYCLE",
  "Driving" = "CAR",
  "Walking + public transport" = c("WALK", "TRANSIT")
)
iso <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(modes), function(label) {
  i <- isochrone(network, park, mode = modes[[label]], cutoffs = c(10, 20, 30),
                 zoom = 11, departure_datetime = departure, time_window = 30)
  i$mode <- label
  i
}))
iso$mode <- factor(iso$mode, levels = names(modes))
st_drop_geometry(iso)
```

The area of each isochrone, in square kilometres, sums up the picture:

```{r areas}
iso$area_km2 <- round(as.numeric(st_area(iso)) / 1e6, 1)
xtabs(area_km2 ~ mode + isochrone, data = st_drop_geometry(iso))
```

## A map

The main streets of the extract give the map some context; the isochrones are
drawn from the largest to the smallest, so that the shorter times stay on top.

```{r map, fig.alt = "Four maps of Porto Alegre, one per mode, with the areas reached from Farroupilha Park within 10, 20 and 30 minutes: a small area walking, a few kilometres around the park cycling, most of the map driving, and long arms along the bus corridors with public transport."}
streets <- st_read(file.path(poa, "poa_osm.pbf"), "lines", quiet = TRUE)
streets <- streets[streets$highway %in% c("motorway", "trunk", "primary",
                                          "secondary", "tertiary"), ]

iso <- iso[order(-iso$isochrone), ]
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = streets, colour = "#dcd3c4", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = iso, aes(fill = factor(isochrone)), colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = st_as_sf(park, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          shape = 21, size = 2.5, fill = "#1f2a2e", colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("10" = "#7a3318", "20" = "#cf7445", "30" = "#e8a57b"),
                    name = "Minutes") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-51.25, -51.14), ylim = c(-30.11, -29.99), datum = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~mode) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

Walking covers a couple of kilometres around the park in half an hour.
Cycling covers no more than walking in the first ten minutes from this park,
then pulls ahead. Driving reaches most of the map within 20 minutes.
Public transport sits in between, and its isochrones follow the bus corridors
leaving the city centre: a stop within a short walk of the park and a fast
ride extend the area far along those lines, and nowhere else.

## People within reach

Polygons answer "where"; a matrix to the hexagonal grid of the sample, which
carries the population of each cell, answers "how many". The share of the
city's population reached from the park, by mode and travel time:

```{r reach}
grid <- read.csv(file.path(poa, "poa_hexgrid.csv"))
reach <- sapply(modes, function(mode) {
  ttm <- travel_time_matrix(network, park, grid, mode = mode,
                            departure_datetime = departure, time_window = 30,
                            max_trip_duration = 60)
  people <- grid$population[match(ttm$to_id, grid$id)]
  sapply(c(15, 30, 45, 60), function(t)
    round(100 * sum(people[ttm$travel_time_p50 <= t]) / sum(grid$population)))
})
rownames(reach) <- paste("within", c(15, 30, 45, 60), "min (%)")
reach
```

```{r reach-figure, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Step curves of the share of the population of Porto Alegre reached from Farroupilha Park within 0 to 60 minutes, by mode: driving reaches nearly everyone within 20 minutes, walking plus public transport most people within an hour, cycling about two thirds and walking about a third."}
fig("reach-by-mode.svg")
```

## Variations

- **Several origins.** Give `isochrone()` more than one point; the `id`
  column tells the polygons apart.
- **Streets instead of areas.** `polygon_output = FALSE` returns the street
  segments reached, each with its travel time, instead of polygons.
- **Traffic stress.** Cycling uses the streets whose level of traffic stress
  is at most `max_lts` (2 by default) and walks the bike on the others. With
  `max_lts = 4`, the 30-minute cycling isochrone from the park grows from
  11.2 to 34.2 km².
- **Uncertainty.** With `percentiles = c(25, 50, 75)`, public transport
  isochrones come in one set per percentile: the area reached on a lucky, a
  typical and an unlucky departure.

The figure on the [home page](../../index.html#gallery) draws the same
isochrones, styled for the documentation, with `site/figures/figures.R` in the
repository.
